title: "QuickSort"

## Simple explanation

QuickSort sorts a list by choosing a pivot value, moving smaller values to
one side and larger values to the other, then repeating the process on each
side.

## Technical explanation

QuickSort is an in-place, divide-and-conquer comparison sort in common
implementations. Its average time complexity is $O(n\log n)$, while an
unbalanced sequence of partitions can produce $O(n^2)$ time. Pivot choice
and partition strategy affect performance and implementation behavior.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Sorting is a common operation in data processing, ranking, and evaluation.
QuickSort illustrates how algorithmic choices affect runtime and why
average-case performance does not remove worst-case considerations.

## How it works

Choose a pivot, partition the range so values fall before or after it, and
recursively sort the partitions. Efficient implementations use small
subarray optimizations and strategies to avoid consistently poor pivots.

## Practical example

Sorting prediction scores can help order results for a ranking task. A
language runtime or library should usually handle the sort; implementing
QuickSort directly is useful mainly for learning or when a specialized
partitioning behavior is required.

## Common misconceptions

- QuickSort is not guaranteed to run in $O(n\log n)$ time on every input.
- “In-place” and stability depend on the exact variant; typical in-place
  QuickSort is not stable.
